name: Valentine Shreve
languages: French (New Orleans riverboat French, fluent and not fit for a drawing room)
equipment: A plum-colored frock coat, a brocade vest with a watch chain and no watch, a clean collar every day somehow
Derringer (Remington over-and-under), 2 rounds loaded, in a vest pocket
Pocket revolver (Smith & Wesson No. 2), 5 rounds loaded, in a coat pocket
Boot knife, in the left boot, which he has never used and would rather not
Playing cards (three decks) and a marked deck, which he swears he carries only for study
A faro dealing box with a spring he can explain if pressed
A pocket edition of Shakespeare, much annotated, quoted wrongly with confidence
Saddle and tack, bedroll, canteen, a carpetbag of good shirts
Riding horse: an elegant, useless chestnut called Bassanio, won at cards
A promissory note for $1,850 to Mrs. Octavia Dumaine of the Silver King faro bank, San Antonio, due 1 July 1874
features: Book Learning (Back East origin: advantage on Investigation checks to read documents, ledgers, deeds, contracts and forgeries; once per long rest he recalls one useful fact about a law, a process or a piece of history; lawyers, bankers and editors treat him as one of their own; disadvantage on his first Riding or Survival check in front of strangers each day)

Read the Table (Gambler: proficiency doubled for Gambling and Insight checks; once per short or long rest, after a minute watching or talking to someone, he learns one thing they are hiding, and the GM tells him the truth of it in a sentence; he always knows whether a game is honest)

Ace in the Hole (Gambler: once per turn, an extra 2d6 damage to one creature he hits with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm, if he has advantage, if another enemy of the target is within 5 ft of it, or if the target believed a lie he told it in the last minute; not part of the damage on his sheet)

Lady Luck (Gambler, 2nd level: 3 luck points per long rest; spend one to roll an extra d20 on an attack, check or save and choose which to use, or to make a creature within 30 ft reroll an attack against him)

Sleeve Gun (Gambler, 2nd level: he draws a concealable weapon as a bonus action unnoticed, has advantage on Sleight of Hand to carry one past a search, and can Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action, which he does often)
Game: Cardsharp (Gambler, 3rd level: he cheats at cards with advantage on the Sleight of Hand check, and once per game a cheat that is spotted can be passed off as the other man's)

Know the Games (Card Sharp background: in any town he finds the best game, the crooked one and the man who runs both within an hour; he knows the house rules and house cheats of poker, faro, monte and chuck-a-luck, and when to leave town)

personality.traits: I talk. I talk beautifully and continuously and to everyone, and I quote Shakespeare, usually Henry the Fifth and usually wrong. I am charming to waiters and cruel to bores. I am a physical coward and I say so first, so that no one else can.
personality.ideals: Everyone is bluffing. The only question at any table is what they are bluffing about, and whether it is worth calling.
personality.bonds: Myself, chiefly. And, though I would never admit it, whoever happens to be riding beside me when the shooting starts; it has happened twice that I did not run, and I am still trying to understand why.
personality.flaws: I owe Mrs. Octavia Dumaine of San Antonio eighteen hundred and fifty dollars, and she has explained, with great courtesy, what happens to the hands of men who do not pay her by the first of July. I would sell my mother for two thousand dollars. I have not yet been asked to sell anyone better.

appearance: A slender, handsome, carefully groomed man of thirty-five with dark hair worn a little long, a waxed moustache, long white hands he protects in kid gloves, and a plum-colored frock coat that has seen better rivers. He sits a horse badly and a chair beautifully.
backstory: Valentine Shreve was born in Baltimore to a shipping family, went to St. Mary's College, was expelled for running a faro bank in the dormitory, and went down the Mississippi on a steamboat in 1858 with forty dollars and a marked deck. He has been a riverboat gambler, a Confederate quartermaster's clerk for eleven months (until he was caught selling the quartermaster's whiskey to both armies), a New Orleans cotton broker's assistant, and a dealer of faro in Galveston, Houston and San Antonio, and he is very good at all of it except leaving the table while he is ahead. In March he lost $1,850 of borrowed money to the Silver King faro bank in San Antonio, and its owner, the formidable Mrs. Octavia Dumaine, has given him until the first of July. He saw the poster in a Waco hotel lobby, did the arithmetic, and bought a horse. He has never caught anyone in his life. He is relying on the others for that. He is relying on himself to notice who at any table is lying, and on this trip, he is going to notice a great deal.
